text: This lab applies everything from this chapter to the three-tier application you've been building since Chapter 1 -- turning a set of CIs and relationships into a complete CSDM chain, from Business Service down to individual CI.

Chapters 1 and 2 built a web server, an application server, and a database server, connected by dependency relationships, with impact analysis already tracing what happens if any one fails. That system never had a name a business stakeholder would recognize -- it existed purely as CIs.

First, name the Business Service: for this scenario, 'Customer Order Processing' -- a name a VP of Sales would recognize, defined by the outcome it provides, not the technology underneath. Second, name the Technical Service that delivers it: the 'Order Processing Application,' the three-tier stack itself, built from the exact CIs Chapters 1 and 2 already modeled. Third, confirm every one of those CIs actually traces upward through that Technical Service with no missing links.

With the chain confirmed, the database server failing can now be described correctly at every altitude from the same underlying fact: at the CI level, the order database server is down; at the Technical Service level, the Order Processing Application is degraded; at the Business Service level, Customer Order Processing is down and customers can't complete orders. Three sentences, one real event, each one correct for the person hearing it.

A model is only finished when the Business Service is named the way the business recognizes it, the Technical Service is genuinely built from real CIs, and every CI traces upward with no gaps -- miss any one of those and impact analysis silently breaks, even though plenty of CIs and relationships still exist somewhere in the CMDB.
That completes Chapter 3. Next, Chapter 4 opens with what Discovery actually does -- the ServiceNow process that finds and populates CMDB data automatically instead of by hand.
